st: Mix the flour and [[0.5 tsp]] of the salt in a bowl. Add the warm water a little at a time until a stiff dough forms.
Knead for 8 minutes until smooth, then cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the lamb, onion, garlic, pepper, caraway, remaining [[1 tsp]] salt and the cold broth with your hand for 2 minutes until sticky and juicy.
Roll the dough into a log and cut into 24 pieces. Roll each into a thin circle about 3.5 inches across.
Put [[1 tbsp]] filling in the center of a circle. Pleat the edge all around, leaving a small hole on top, so it looks like a little purse.
Lightly oil a steamer basket or line it with parchment. Set the buuz inside without letting them touch.
Steam over boiling water, covered, for 20 minutes. Work in batches if needed.
Check that the filling reaches 160°F (71°C). Serve hot, with the juices inside.
Stir the flour with [[0.5 tsp]] of the salt, then add the warm water to make a firm dough. Knead 5 minutes, then cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the lamb, onion, garlic, pepper, remaining [[1 tsp]] salt and the cold water until sticky.
Divide the dough into 12 balls and roll each into a thin circle about 5 inches across.
Spoon about [[3 tbsp]] filling onto one half of each circle, leaving a border.
Fold over to make a half moon. Press the edge to seal, then crimp with a fork or pleat the edge.
Heat the oil in a deep skillet to 350°F (175°C).
Fry 3 or 4 at a time for 3 minutes per side until deep golden and the meat is cooked to 160°F (71°C).
Drain on paper towels and serve hot.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Wash the stones, set them on a baking sheet, and heat them in the oven for 45 minutes. Never use river stones or damp or porous stones, because they can crack.
Cut the lamb into serving pieces and toss with the salt and pepper.
In a large heavy lidded pot (a Dutch oven works), layer the lamb and onions with the water.
Add a layer of hot stones using tongs, then the potatoes, carrots and cabbage.
Add the remaining stones on top, keeping some for the center.
Cover tightly and cook over low heat for 90 minutes. Do not open the lid in the first hour.
Check that the lamb reaches 145°F (63°C) and is tender and the vegetables are soft.
Use tongs to remove the stones. Serve the meat and vegetables with the juices. Traditionally people pass the hot stones from hand to hand, but handle them only with care.
Mix the flour with [[0.5 tsp]] of the salt and the water to form a firm dough. Knead 5 minutes, brush with a little oil, cover, and rest for 30 minutes.
Roll the dough out as thin as you can, about 1/8 inch, and cut into noodles about 1/4 inch wide.
Boil the noodles in salted water for 3 minutes, then drain and toss with [[1 tbsp]] of oil. Alternatively, steam them for 10 minutes.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a large wok or skillet over high heat. Stir-fry the beef for 3 minutes until browned.
Add the onion and garlic for 2 minutes, then the carrots for 3 minutes.
Add the cabbage, remaining [[1 tsp]] salt and the pepper and cook for 4 minutes.
Add the noodles and broth. Toss well and cook for 4 minutes until the noodles absorb the liquid and start to brown.
Serve hot straight from the pan.

ing: bone-in, cut into pieces; or lamb
st: Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) and heat the clean stones on a tray for 45 minutes.
Rub the goat with the salt, pepper and garlic.
Put the goat, onions and water in a heavy lidded roasting pot or large Dutch oven, since a whole animal is not practical at home.
Add 3 hot stones with tongs, then the potatoes and carrots.
Place the remaining stones on top, then seal with a lid and foil.
Cook at 325°F (160°C) for 90 minutes without opening.
Check that the goat reaches 145°F (63°C) and is tender.
Remove the stones with tongs and serve the meat with the vegetables and juices.
Heat the oil in a big pot over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb for 6 minutes.
Add the onion and garlic and cook for 4 minutes.
Pour in the water, add the salt and pepper, and bring to a boil. Skim off any foam.
Cover and simmer on low for 45 minutes until the lamb is tender.
Add the carrots and potatoes and simmer for 12 minutes.
Add the noodles and cook for 5 minutes until tender.
Taste and adjust the salt. Stir in the dill and serve hot.
Mix the flour, [[0.25 tsp]] of the salt and the warm water into a firm dough. Knead 5 minutes, cover, and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the lamb, onion, garlic, pepper, remaining [[1 tsp]] salt and the cold water into a sticky filling.
Roll the dough thin and cut out circles about 2.5 inches wide.
Place about [[2 tsp]] filling on each circle, fold it in half, and pinch the edge closed, making small dumplings.
Bring a big pot of salted water to a boil and cook the dumplings in batches.
Boil for 8 minutes until they float and the filling reaches 160°F (71°C).
Meanwhile, heat the tea or broth in another pot until hot.
Serve the dumplings in bowls of the hot broth or tea, or on a plate with a little of the cooking liquid.
Whisk the egg, sugar, milk and melted butter in a bowl.
In another bowl, mix the flour, baking powder and salt, then add the wet mixture.
Mix and knead briefly to make a soft dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
On a floured surface, roll the dough about 1/2 inch thick.
Cut into diamonds, rectangles or small twists about 2 inches long.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 350°F (175°C).
Fry in small batches for 3 minutes, turning once, until golden brown.
Drain on paper towels and cool for 10 minutes. Dust with powdered sugar if you like.
Bring the water to a boil in a saucepan.
Add the tea and simmer for 3 minutes until the water is dark.
Strain out the tea leaves if you wish, or leave them for a stronger tea.
Pour in the milk and stir.
Heat gently to a near simmer for 5 minutes. Lift the milk with a ladle now and then to cool it and make it frothy.
Stir in the butter and salt until the butter melts.
Add the rice if using. Taste and adjust the salt, then serve hot in bowls.
